chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
title: Poor tunes, Eddie King and the push to sound like Whiteman
summary: Management assigned weak pop tunes and singers and wanted a Whiteman-style band, suppressing Bix; Sunday and My Pretty Girl were the exceptions.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: That's right, the place was loaded. And our band got along well. So I'm still waiting for arrangements to make the records and they come up with some dillies. Like 'I'M Looking Over a Four-Leaf Clover,' 'Idolizing' and a waltz thing called 'Hushabye' and oh, I don't know, they came up with several things like that, which in their own way are good tunes, but what they were trying to do was make the band popular. And besides, we had Eddie King there who was trying to suppress

the band. He didn't want any part of Bix. He didn't want any part of the jazz part of the band. He wanted it to be another Whiteman band, something which he was very successful with. and Eddie King, you know, he and Whiteman and Grofé were like that, all in one, and that was the (sings) which I'm a great favorite of, the oompha at that time, it's kept a good tempo, but that was Grofé's (phonetic) style and it was a style of the Whiteman band.

We had a more, aloofal style, and you couldn't make the one, ours go over into their type of thing, which had been very, very successful. So they come up, they're thinking the tunes can do it. They tried, but they didn't come up with anything. The first tune we got that was like anything like what we could do was "Sunday" and then they brought us a trio. They also picked out our singers, so we had Bix Murray, Frank Bessinger, guys like that although good in their own, they were successful, weren't good with us. And then they brought this trio in, a real fo-dodeo type of thing and -- but they did bring Joe and Eddie in, which they figured would -- "We won't use Bix but we'll use Joe and Eddie.

Now that's more improvising than you can get, but it's a different kind of improvising. Eddie King could probably go along with. It didn't hurt anything. So here we got Eddie right in front of the mike playing his guitar and we got a hell of a fine banjo player down there, Howdy Quicksell and

you don't even hear him. You know, they just ran roughshod over some of the things that we had that we could do. Later on we did 'My Pretty Girl' and it was liked by the musicians, which, I guess, that's what we were trying to satisfy and we were trying to make something that would impress the musicians.

The dance public in those days, anyway, it was a different dance public. It wasn't like the kind that would go into the Paramount and clap and scream like Benny Goodman had, which came along with swing. This was the old jazz and to try to impress them you had to things like the slide whistle and some of the tricks that Whiteman had, he had it made and besides they got all good tunes, and besides Shilkret got all the other good tunes. And Roger Kahn got the 'Blue Room' to do. We would have liked to have done Blue Room but Roger, you know, had a little club. He had his own club and he had a hell of a band.

Tommy Gott, Arnold Brilhant, Alfie Alphie Evans and Joe and Eddie. He had a real crackerjack band. We used to go over and listen to it. But these were angles that we couldn't seem to get by. So we went back to Detroit and let's say with out tail between our legs, but we were pretty sure -- waiting for the tunes to come out, nothing happened, but 'Sunday' gave us a little kick, but that was the only one.
